title: Q3 Product Roadmap Sync
description: Reviewing Q3 commitments ahead of the board update.
transcript: Good morning everyone. Let's get started — I know Raj can't make it, so I'll send him a summary afterwards.
Agenda is short today. Q3 pricing, the API rate limit incident from last week, and then where we actually are on the mobile onboarding work.
Morning. Before we start — do we want to talk about the hiring req as well, or is that a separate conversation?
Separate. Let's keep this one to the roadmap, otherwise we'll run over again like last time.
Okay. Pricing. Aisha, you pulled the numbers — do you want to walk us through what you found?
Sure. So I looked at the last two quarters of usage across the enterprise tier, and the short version is that our seat-based model is leaving money on the table.
The top decile of accounts are using roughly four times the API volume of the median account, but they're paying the same per seat.
Do we know if that's a handful of outliers or a real distribution?
It's a real distribution. It's not one whale skewing it. There are about thirty accounts in that band and they've all grown volume month over month since February.
That tracks with what we're seeing on the infrastructure side. The cost curve on those accounts is genuinely uncomfortable.
So the proposal is usage-based billing for enterprise. Chloe, what's the read from marketing?
Cautiously positive. The thing I'd want to avoid is a repeat of the 2024 migration where people found out about a pricing change from a billing email.
If we do this, we need at minimum sixty days' notice and a calculator on the pricing page so people can model their own bill.
Is the calculator a design ask? Because if so I'd like to know now rather than in three weeks.
It is, sorry. I should have flagged that earlier.
It's fine, I'd just rather have it in the plan than sprung on us.
Noted. Priya, can you scope the calculator this week? Even a rough estimate.
Yeah, I can have something by Thursday.
One thing I want to raise — what happens to the accounts that are currently underpaying relative to usage? Do they get an immediate increase?
That's the part I don't have a good answer to yet.
My instinct is we grandfather existing contracts through to renewal. It's slower revenue but it avoids a churn spike.
I'd back that. The optics of a mid-contract increase are bad enough that I think it costs us more than it earns.
How long is 'through to renewal' in practice? Some of those contracts are eighteen months.
Median remaining term is about seven months. There are four accounts past twelve.
Then let's cap it. Grandfathered for two quarters, and the four long-tail accounts we handle individually.
Okay, so — decision. Enterprise moves to usage-based billing, existing customers grandfathered for two quarters, sixty days' notice, calculator ships with the announcement.
Aisha, can you own the model? I need a revenue projection for the board deck.
Yep. When do you need it?
Board's on the fourteenth, so I'd want it by the ninth to have time to argue with it.
Right. Let's move to the API incident. Marcus?
So — last Tuesday, around eleven in the morning, we started rate limiting a chunk of legitimate traffic.
The root cause was a config change that dropped the per-account limit from ten thousand requests an hour to one thousand. It was meant to apply to trial accounts only.
Forty minutes. We caught it because two customers opened tickets within about ten minutes of each other.
Northwind and one of the mid-market accounts. Elena's already spoken to Northwind.
That's the second config-related incident this quarter.
It is, and I'm not going to defend it. The underlying problem is that config changes don't go through review the way code does.
Anyone with production access can change a limit and it takes effect immediately. There's no staging step and no approval.
What would it take to fix that properly?
Two weeks of one engineer, roughly. Put the config in version control, require a pull request, and add a canary rollout so a bad change hits five percent of traffic first.
Would that have caught this one?
The canary would have. Five percent of accounts hitting a rate limit is noise; a hundred percent is an incident.
Two weeks is a lot in a quarter where we're also doing a pricing migration.
I know. But we've now had two of these, and the next one might land during the pricing announcement, which is exactly when we can't afford it.
For what it's worth, this is the kind of thing that shows up in support volume for weeks afterwards even when the incident itself is short.
Okay. Marcus, put together a one-pager — scope, who does it, what slips. I'd rather make that trade-off explicitly than let it get squeezed out.
Last thing. Mobile onboarding. Priya, where are we actually?
Honestly? Behind. The design is done and I'm happy with it, but we've been blocked on the auth flow for about two weeks.
That's partly on us. James has been pulled onto the incident work.
I'm not blaming anyone, I just don't want us to get to the end of the quarter and act surprised.
No, that's the right instinct. What's the realistic date?
If James is back on it next week, we could be in internal testing by the end of the month. If not, it slips to Q4.
I can get James back on it Monday. The incident work is mostly writing things down at this point.
Then let's do that. Priya, can you and Marcus sync on Monday and give me a date I can put in the board deck?
One question on onboarding — is the new flow going to change anything customer-facing that I need to write about?
The signup flow gets shorter. Four steps down to two. That's probably worth a blog post.
Definitely worth a blog post. I'll put it in the content calendar.
Good. Let's wrap. Aisha's got the revenue model by the ninth, Marcus has the config one-pager by Friday, Priya's scoping the calculator by Thursday and syncing with Marcus Monday.

summary.overview: The team confirmed the move to usage-based billing for the enterprise tier, with existing contracts grandfathered for two quarters and a sixty-day notice period. Marcus reported on the API rate-limit incident, which was caused by an unreviewed config change, and was asked to scope a two-week fix putting configuration behind pull-request review with canary rollout. Mobile onboarding is behind by roughly two weeks because James was pulled onto incident work; he returns to it Monday, with a firm date expected before the board meeting.
summary.gist: Pricing moves to usage-based; config review work scoped; mobile onboarding at risk but recoverable.

bullets: Top decile of enterprise accounts use ~4× the API volume of the median but pay the same per seat.
About thirty accounts sit in that band, all growing month over month since February — a distribution, not an outlier.
Enterprise tier moves to usage-based billing.
Sixty days' notice and a self-serve pricing calculator are conditions of the change, not nice-to-haves.
Existing contracts grandfathered for two quarters to avoid a churn spike.
Median remaining term is seven months; four accounts run past twelve and will be handled individually.
A config change intended for trial accounts dropped the per-account limit from 10,000 to 1,000 requests/hour.
Live for forty minutes; detected via two customer tickets rather than monitoring.
Config changes bypass review entirely — no staging, no approval, immediate effect.
Proposed fix: version-controlled config, pull-request review, canary rollout to 5% of traffic.
Estimated at two engineer-weeks; a canary would have caught this incident.
Design complete; blocked roughly two weeks on the auth flow.
James returns to the work Monday; internal testing by month end if unblocked, otherwise slips to Q4.
Signup shortens from four steps to two — worth a launch post.

action_items.text: Build the revenue projection model for the usage-based pricing change
Write a one-pager scoping the config review and canary rollout work
Sync on mobile onboarding and commit to a date for the board deck
Add the shortened signup flow to the content calendar
Send Raj a written summary of the pricing decision
